abstract: Microbial remineralisation of sinking particles governs the depth and magnitude of organic carbon sequestration in the ocean. Yet, the combined influence of environmental gradients and particle morphology in regulating remineralisation remains poorly constrained. During spring in the subpolar Icelandic Basin, we estimated microbial carbon turnover, a proxy for remineralization, on fast sinking particles collected at two depths below the mixed-layer using shipboard incubations. Alongside this we used imagery to determine the morphology and complexity of the particles. Microbial carbon turnover exhibited strong depth-dependent variability, with generally higher rates in shallower samples and substantial variability among stations and sampling days. Fast-sinking particle assemblages were dominated by aggregates and detrital material, while faecal pellets comprised only a minor fraction of particles, and particle diversity decreased with depth. Environmental variables, particularly chlorophyll-a concentration, explained over 80% of observed variability in microbial carbon turnover. Particle traits describing size, size heterogeneity and structural complexity were also significant predictors, increasing model explanatory power to 91%. Larger and more heterogeneous particle assemblages were associated with lower microbial carbon turnover, while increased structural complexity was associated with lower turnover after accounting for particle size. Together these findings indicate that particle traits provide additional controls on microbial carbon turnover beyond environmental variables alone.
